deep.reconstruction:
Context: the previous page ends a statement of the form (m/M) = ε (M/m) with ε = i^{bB/2}, which is the biquadratic reciprocity law for Gaussian integers. This page begins a numbered sequence of definitions (§§1–3) for a lattice-point counting symbol [p,p'] for complex numbers p, p'. It appears to be the counting tool for a lattice-point (Eisenstein-style) treatment of that law, in which the third-proof/Eisenstein count for quadratic reciprocity is lifted to Gaussian integers. The page itself contains only definitions, no theorem.

§1. Let i = sqrt(-1), p = x+iy and p' = x'+iy'. Assume first that y and y' are positive and that x'−x > 0. Let L(X) = [y(x'−X) + y'(X−x)]/(x'−x) be the straight line (chord) from (x,y) to (x',y'). Define [p,p'] as the number of integer pairs (X,Y) with x < X ≤ x' and 0 < Y ≤ L(X). The 'former' (lower) limits x and 0 are excluded and the 'latter' (upper) limits x' and L(X) are included.

Gauss restates this as four sign conditions: X−x > 0, Y > 0, x'−X ≥ 0, and y(x'−X) + y'(X−x) + Y(x−x') ≥ 0. The last condition is equivalent to Y ≤ L(X) after dividing by x'−x > 0. This step is mine to check, and it holds.

Hence, in modern form (my restatement): [p,p'] = Σ_{X integer, x<X≤x'} floor(L(X)). This is the number of lattice points in the trapezoid under the segment p p', with the left edge and the X-axis excluded and the right edge and the top edge included.

§2. The symbol is extended to the degenerate and reversed cases:
- if x' = x, set [p,p'] = 0;
- if x' < x, set [p,p'] = −[p',p].
This makes the symbol an oriented (antisymmetric) quantity, like a line integral.

§3. After §2 the only remaining restriction is that y and y' be non-negative; for negative ordinates the counting definition is meaningless as it stands. Choose an integer n so large that y+n and y'+n are positive. The definition continues on the next page: [p,p'] := [p+in, p'+in] − n[x'] + n[x], where [·] is Gauss's floor bracket.

This is independent of n, which is my verification. Shifting the line up by an integer n raises floor(L(X)) by exactly n at each of the floor(x')−floor(x) integers X in (x,x']. Therefore [p+in, p'+in] = [p,p'] + n([x']−[x]).

The resulting general definition is the signed sum [p,p'] = Σ_{x<X≤x'} floor(L(X)) for arbitrary real ordinates, oriented by the sign of x'−x. The theorems on the next page (shift by integers, additivity along collinear points, decomposition modulo a Gaussian integer P) are the expected next steps toward a counting proof of the reciprocity law.
errors: No mathematical errors on this page. The verbal description ('first limits excluded, last included') and the inequality form agree: X−x>0, Y>0, x'−X≥0, and line−Y≥0 (since x−x'<0).

Next-page context, not this page: the definition is correctly [p,p'] = [p+in, p'+in] − n[x'] + n[x]. However, Lehrsatz I as transcribed, [p+ni, p'+ni] = [p,p'] − n[x'] + n[x], has the wrong sign; it should read + n[x'] − n[x]. This is either a slip by Gauss or a transcription error. The transcription also has 'p+in' where 'p'+in' is meant in the second argument.

results.what: Definition of [p,p'] as the number of lattice points under the chord from (x,y) to (x',y'), i.e. Σ_{x<X≤x'} floor(L(X)), with half-open boundary conventions
results.modern_name: Lattice-point count under a line segment / generalized Dedekind-type floor sum (trapezoid lattice count)
results.usually_credited_to: Lattice-point counting for reciprocity: Gauss (3rd proof, 1808, floor bracket [x]) and Eisenstein (geometric lattice proof, 1844)
